item.title: Generalization Theory, PAC Learning, and the Modern Over-parameterization Paradigm
item.description:
Foundations of Generalization: Hypothesis Space & Risk Formulations

Supervised machine learning seeks a predictive mapping $h: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ within a predefined function family that minimizes discrepancy on unobserved data.

Demystifying $h$ and $\mathcal{H}$: Connecting Parameters to Functions

In neural networks and regression, model architectures are defined by parameter collections (weights and biases) $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\mathbf{w}, b) \in \mathbb{R}^P$, where $P$ denotes the total count of scalar parameters:

$$ h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b) \quad \text{or} \quad h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}^{(L)} \dots \sigma(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}) $$

  • A Concrete Hypothesis ($h \in \mathcal{H}$): An instantiated function where all weights $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ are fixed to concrete numerical constants. For example, $h_1(\mathbf{x}) = 2x_1 - 3$ and $h_2(\mathbf{x}) = -0.5x_1 + 4$ represent two distinct hypotheses.

  • The Hypothesis Space ($\mathcal{H}$): The set of all possible candidate functions expressible by the given model architecture across all permissible parameter values:

$$ \mathcal{H} \triangleq \{ h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^P \} $$

Notation Breakdown:

  • $\triangleq$ denotes “defined as” (definitional equality, not an algebraically derived equality).
  • $\{ \text{output} \mid \text{condition} \}$ is standard set-builder notation (“the set of all $h_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ such that $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ satisfies the condition”).
  • $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^P$ specifies that the parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is chosen from a $P$-dimensional continuous real vector space ($P$ is the total number of tunable weights).

Pedagogical Simplification in Introductory Lectures: In elementary examples (e.g., classifying Pokemon via simple thresholds), the hypothesis space is artificially discretized into a finite set (e.g., $|\mathcal{H}| = 10\,000$) purely to illustrate basic counting before introducing continuous calculus.

Empirical Risk vs. Expected (True) Risk

Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the unknown true distribution of the underlying physical phenomenon generating pairs $(\mathbf{x}, y) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$.

  • Expected Risk (True Loss over Unseen Reality): The theoretical average error evaluated across all potential samples that nature could ever generate:
$$ L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}}) \triangleq \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y) \sim \mathcal{D}} [\ell(h(\mathbf{x}), y)] $$

Notation Breakdown:

  • $\mathbb{E}$ denotes the mathematical Expectation (the true statistical population average).

  • $(\mathbf{x}, y) \sim \mathcal{D}$ denotes that instances are randomly drawn according to the underlying natural probability distribution $\mathcal{D}$.

  • $\ell(h(\mathbf{x}), y)$ (lowercase script $\ell$) denotes the single-sample loss (e.g., the squared error $(h(\mathbf{x}) - y)^2$ evaluated on one specific observation).

  • Empirical Risk (Training Loss over Observed Data): The computable arithmetic mean evaluated over a finite training dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} = \{(\mathbf{x}^{(n)}, y^{(n)})\}_{n=1}^N$:

$$ L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) \triangleq \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^N \ell(h(\mathbf{x}^{(n)}), y^{(n)}) $$

Definition of a Representative Dataset

An empirical training sample $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$ is defined as $\varepsilon$-representative (or simply “good”) if the empirical training loss uniformly mirrors the expected true risk across every single candidate in $\mathcal{H}$:

$$ \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \text{ is good} \iff \forall h \in \mathcal{H}, \quad |L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) - L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}})| \le \varepsilon $$

Theorem (Uniform Generalization Guarantee). If $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$ is $\varepsilon$-representative, then the empirical risk minimizer $h^{\text{train}} \triangleq \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}})$ closely tracks the performance of the theoretical best-in-class hypothesis $h^{\text{all}} \triangleq \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}})$:

$$ L(h^{\text{train}}, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}}) - L(h^{\text{all}}, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}}) \le 2\varepsilon $$

Proof. By the definition of uniform convergence:

$$ \begin{aligned} L(h^{\text{train}}, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}}) &\le L(h^{\text{train}}, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) + \varepsilon \\ &\le L(h^{\text{all}}, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) + \varepsilon \quad (\text{since } h^{\text{train}} \text{ minimizes empirical loss}) \\ &\le \left( L(h^{\text{all}}, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}}) + \varepsilon \right) + \varepsilon = L(h^{\text{all}}, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}}) + 2\varepsilon \end{aligned} $$

$\blacksquare$

The PAC Framework: Demystifying $\varepsilon$, $\delta$, and Sample Complexity

The foundational paradigm of theoretical machine learning is PAC Learning (Probably Approximately Correct), introduced by Leslie Valiant. It acknowledges that because empirical data is randomly drawn from nature, absolute mathematical certainty is impossible.

Definition (PAC Learnability). A hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ is PAC-learnable if there exists an algorithm such that for any distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and any arbitrary tolerances $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$ and $\delta \in (0, 1)$, given $N \ge N(\varepsilon, \delta)$ samples, the algorithm outputs a hypothesis $\hat{h}$ satisfying:

$$ P\Big( L(\hat{h}, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}}) - \min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}}) \le \varepsilon \Big) \ge 1 - \delta $$

Dual Interpretations of $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$:

  • $\varepsilon$ (Accuracy Tolerance / Precision Margin): Governs how approximately correct the solution must be. It dictates the maximum permissible discrepancy between empirical observation and global reality.
  • $\delta$ (Confidence Failure Risk): Governs how probable catastrophic failure is. Because samples are stochastic, there is always a non-zero probability of drawing pathological, unrepresentative outliers. $\delta$ sets the strict upper bound on this disaster probability (i.e., confidence is at least $1 - \delta$).

Inverting the Hoeffding Bound into Sample Complexity. By setting the worst-case failure probability upper bound to not exceed $\delta$:

$$ P(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \text{ is bad}) \le 2|\mathcal{H}| \exp\left(-2N\varepsilon^2\right) \le \delta $$

Solving analytically for the sample size $N$ yields the fundamental Sample Complexity:

$$ -2N\varepsilon^2 \le \ln\left(\frac{\delta}{2|\mathcal{H}|}\right) \iff 2N\varepsilon^2 \ge \ln\left(\frac{2|\mathcal{H}|}{\delta}\right) \iff N \ge \frac{1}{2\varepsilon^2} \left( \ln(2|\mathcal{H}|) + \ln\frac{1}{\delta} \right) $$

The Engineering Reality: The required data volume scales quadratically with precision demand ($\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon^2)$), logarithmically with model class cardinality ($\ln|\mathcal{H}|$), and logarithmically with safety confidence ($\ln(1/\delta)$).

From Discrete Counting to Continuous Parameters

The Discrete Setting: Hoeffding’s Inequality & Union Bound

For a bounded loss $\ell \in [0, 1]$, Hoeffding’s inequality guarantees that for any individual, frozen hypothesis $h$:

$$ P\left( |L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) - L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}})| > \varepsilon \right) \le 2\exp\left(-2N\varepsilon^2\right) $$

To ensure that no candidate model in a discrete space $\mathcal{H}$ fails, applying Boole’s inequality (Union Bound) produces:

$$ \begin{aligned} P(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \text{ is bad}) &= P\left( \bigcup_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \left\{ |L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) - L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}})| > \varepsilon \right\} \right) \\ &\le \sum_{h \in \mathcal{H}} P\left( |L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) - L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{all}})| > \varepsilon \right) \\ &\le |\mathcal{H}| \cdot 2\exp(-2N\varepsilon^2) \end{aligned} $$

Numerical Mechanics ($|\mathcal{H}|=10\,000, \varepsilon=0.1$):

  • $N=100 \implies P(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \text{ is bad}) \le 10\,000 \times 2\exp(-2) \approx 2707$. The bound is statistically trivial (vacuous) because true probability cannot exceed $1$. It signifies that statistical theory cannot guarantee generalization when sample volume $N$ is dwarfed by candidate capacity $|\mathcal{H}|$.
  • $N=1000 \implies P(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \text{ is bad}) \le 10\,000 \times 2\exp(-20) \le 0.00004$ (generalization is guaranteed with $99.996\%$ confidence).

The Continuous Dilemma: Why Naive Counting Breaks ($|\mathcal{H}| = \infty$)

In real regression models and neural networks, parameters $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^P$ are continuous real numbers. Consequently, the set of expressible hypotheses is uncountably infinite:

$$ |\mathcal{H}| = \infty \implies P(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \text{ is bad}) \le \infty \cdot 2\exp(-2N\varepsilon^2) = \infty $$

The discrete Union Bound collapses in continuous parameter settings, necessitating an alternative way to measure functional capacity.

The Geometric Resolution: Effective Dichotomies & VC-Dimension

The resolution lies in a geometric observation: infinite continuous hypotheses exhibit strictly finite behavior when projected onto $N$ discrete data points.

Figure 1 — Although continuous parameters admit infinite candidate lines, the number of distinct binary label assignments (dichotomies) on $N$ points is strictly bounded.

Definition (Growth Function). Let $\mathcal{H}$ act on $N$ inputs $S = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N\}$. The Growth Function $m_{\mathcal{H}}(N)$ measures the maximum number of distinct binary labelings achievable across any $N$ points:

$$ m_{\mathcal{H}}(N) \triangleq \max_{\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N} |\{ (h(\mathbf{x}_1), \dots, h(\mathbf{x}_N)) \mid h \in \mathcal{H} \}| \le 2^N $$

Definition (Vapnik-Chervonenkis Dimension). The VC-dimension $d_{\text{VC}}$ is the maximum sample size $N$ for which the model can realize all $2^N$ possible binary label combinations (i.e., shatter the points). For a linear model in $\mathbb{R}^D$, $d_{\text{VC}} = D + 1$.

Lemma (Sauer-Shelah). Once sample volume $N$ exceeds the VC-dimension $d_{\text{VC}}$, the growth function stops expanding exponentially and becomes bounded by a polynomial:

$$ m_{\mathcal{H}}(N) \le \left( \frac{eN}{d_{\text{VC}}} \right)^{d_{\text{VC}}} = \mathcal{O}\left( N^{d_{\text{VC}}} \right) $$

Theorem (Vapnik-Chervonenkis Generalization Bound). Replacing $|\mathcal{H}|$ with the polynomial growth function gives the unified continuous guarantee:

$$ P(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \text{ is bad}) \le 4 \underbrace{\left( \frac{2eN}{d_{\text{VC}}} \right)^{d_{\text{VC}}}}_{\text{Polynomial Growth } \mathcal{O}(N^d)} \cdot \underbrace{\exp\left( -\frac{1}{8} N \varepsilon^2 \right)}_{\text{Exponential Decay } \mathcal{O}(e^{-N})} $$

Core Intuition: Even though continuous parameters create an infinite number of candidate functions ($|\mathcal{H}| = \infty$), their ability to generate distinct outputs on $N$ points grows only polynomially ($\mathcal{O}(N^{d_{\text{VC}}})$). Because exponential decay asymptotically dominates any polynomial rate, the error bound vanishes to zero as sample size $N \to \infty$.

Model Selection, Validation Pitfalls, and the Nature of Overfitting

Model Selection as Training: The Validation Bound

In practice, machine learning workflows train several competing candidate architectures (or hyperparameter configurations) $\mathcal{H}_1, \mathcal{H}_2, \dots, \mathcal{H}_M$ on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$, yielding candidate models:

$$ h_m^* = \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}_m} L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}), \quad m \in \{1, \dots, M\} $$

To select the best model, practitioners evaluate them against an independent validation set $\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}$:

$$ h^* = \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}_{\text{val}}} L(h, \mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}), \quad \text{where } \mathcal{H}_{\text{val}} \triangleq \{h_1^*, h_2^*, \dots, h_M^*\} $$

The Critical Theoretical Insight: Evaluating and selecting a model using a validation set is mathematically equivalent to empirical risk minimization on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}$ over the hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}_{\text{val}}$. Applying Hoeffding’s inequality over the validation pool yields:

$$ P(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}} \text{ is bad}) \le |\mathcal{H}_{\text{val}}| \cdot 2\exp\left(-2 N_{\text{val}} \varepsilon^2\right) $$

The Benchmark Paradox: Peeking & Overfitting to the Validation Set

This formulation reveals a counter-intuitive engineering truth:

  • The Risk of Large Candidate Pools ($|\mathcal{H}_{\text{val}}| \to \infty$): If an engineer benchmarks thousands of hyperparameter configurations against the same validation set, the likelihood that at least one mediocre model gets an outstanding validation score purely by stochastic luck approaches $1$.
  • Human as Optimizer: Continual manual tuning based on validation feedback effectively turns the human engineer into an outer-loop optimization algorithm, causing the model family to overfit to $\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}$ (Data Leakage through Peeking).
  • The Candidate Reduction Dilemma: While shrinking $|\mathcal{H}_{\text{val}}|$ mathematically tightens the bound, arbitrarily discarding models risks excluding the true optimal model (incurring high Approximation Error).
  • The True Solution ($N_{\text{val}}$ Scaling): Because validation bounds scale exponentially with validation size $\exp(-2 N_{\text{val}} \varepsilon^2)$ but only linearly with pool size $|\mathcal{H}_{\text{val}}|$, increasing validation sample volume (e.g., via $K$-fold cross-validation) is mathematically superior to artificially restricting experimentation.

A Rigorous Definition of Overfitting

Overfitting is often colloquially confused with “zero training error” or “model complexity”. In statistical learning theory, overfitting has an exact, comparative definition:

Definition (Overfitting as Relative Degradation). Given two hypotheses $h_1, h_2 \in \mathcal{H}$, hypothesis $h_2$ is said to overfit relative to $h_1$ if and only if:

$$ L(h_2, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) < L(h_1, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}) \quad \text{and} \quad L(h_2, \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}) > L(h_1, \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}) $$

Three-Way Diagnostic Framework:

  1. Underfitting (High Bias / Approximation Error): Both training error and test error are large ($L_{\text{train}} \gg 0, L_{\text{test}} \gg 0$). The model family lacks the expressive capacity to fit the underlying phenomenon.
  2. Overfitting (High Variance / Estimation Error): Training error is exceptionally low, but the generalization gap diverges ($L_{\text{train}} \approx 0, L_{\text{test}} \gg 0$). The model has memorized sample-specific stochastic noise rather than generalizable signals.
  3. Data Mismatch (Covariate Shift): Training error is low, test error is high, but the cause is that the underlying generating distributions differ ($\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} \ne \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}$). This is a domain shift problem, unresolvable by statistical regularization.

Epistemological Synthesis: Subjectivity Under Mathematical Discipline

Machine learning cannot eliminate human subjectivity:

  • Setting $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ reflects subjective human risk tolerance.
  • Choosing an inductive architecture (e.g., CNNs vs. Transformers) reflects human physical priors about the world.

However, statistical learning theory transforms subjective choices from arbitrary guessing into disciplined engineering: it establishes the exact mathematical cost ($N \ge N(\varepsilon, \delta, \mathcal{H})$) required to guarantee that human priors do not lead to unmitigated failure.

The Modern Resolution: The Double Descent Phenomenon

Classical learning theory establishes that increasing capacity beyond sample size causes divergence in test error. However, modern deep neural networks operate with parameter counts orders of magnitude larger than training data ($P \gg N$), reaching exact interpolation ($L_{\text{train}} = 0$) while maintaining strong generalization.

Figure 2 — The double descent phenomenon: test error peaks at the interpolation threshold ($P \approx N$) where noise forced into minimal capacity causes erratic oscillation, but monotonically declines deep in the over-parameterized regime ($P \gg N$).

Why Over-parameterization Generalizes: Three Core Pillars

When $P \gg N$, there exist infinitely many parameter configurations that achieve zero empirical training error ($L_{\text{train}} = 0$). Why do neural networks pick a solution that generalizes well rather than an erratic, memorizing interpolant? Generalization is governed by three underlying physical and mathematical pillars.

Pillar 1: Implicit Regularization of Gradient Descent (“Lazy Optimization”)

When a parameter space has infinite zero-loss global minima, the optimization algorithm itself acts as a selector:

  • Minimal Euclidean Norm Preference: For linear regression initialized at the origin $\mathbf{w}_0 = \mathbf{0}$, gradient descent provably converges to the minimum $L_2$-norm solution:
$$ \mathbf{w}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \|\mathbf{w}\|_2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{y} $$

A smaller weight norm directly translates to smaller geometric slopes ($\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f$), preventing extreme fluctuations between adjacent sample points.

  • Flat Minima in Deep Networks: In non-linear deep models, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) paired with mini-batch noise inherently avoids narrow, steep valleys and gravitates toward wide, flat minima. A flat basin ensures that small perturbations or distribution shifts between training and test sets produce minimal changes in prediction.

Pillar 2: Structural Inductive Bias (“Architectural Constraints”)

Counting raw parameters vastly overstates a network’s true functional flexibility. Model architectures impose physical structural priors on what functions are reachable:

  • Spatial Locality (CNNs): Convolutional filters operate only over small local patches ($3 \times 3$) and tie weights across the entire image. This architectural constraint makes it structurally impossible for a CNN to represent chaotic functions that treat pixels independently.
  • Relational Permutation Equivariance (Transformers): Self-attention matrices constrain interactions to pairwise relational affinities, enforcing symmetry over token sets.
  • Hierarchical Modularity (Deep Composition): A deep composition $f(\mathbf{x}) = f_L(\dots f_1(\mathbf{x}))$ constrains representations to low-dimensional smooth manifolds, strictly ruling out high-entropy random memorizers from the reachable hypothesis search space.

Pillar 3: Spectral Bias & The Frequency Principle (“Coarse-to-Fine”)

Neural networks do not learn all patterns at equal speed; they learn frequencies hierarchically:

$$ \text{Global, low-frequency patterns} \xrightarrow{\text{Learned First}} \text{High-frequency localized variations} \xrightarrow{\text{Learned Late}} $$
  • The Frequency Principle: Under gradient descent, the lower Fourier frequency components of the target function are fitted rapidly, whereas high-frequency variations (including random label noise) take exponentially more gradient steps to learn.
  • Benign Overfitting: Even when a massive network is trained until it perfectly interpolates noisy observations, the over-parameterized weights accommodate those points with localized, minimal-energy adjustments, leaving the global smooth landscape intact.

Summary: Paradigm Comparison

Dimension Classical Learning Theory Modern Deep Learning Paradigm
Capacity Metric Raw Parameter Count ($P$), VC-dimension Effective Capacity constrained by Inductive Bias
Continuous Space Handled via VC-dichotomy Handled via Implicit Geometric Regularization
Optimization View Passive solver of fixed convex objective Active implicit regularizer (Minimum-norm bias)
Target Regime Under-parameterized ($P < N$) Heavily over-parameterized ($P \gg N$)
Overfitting Behavior Capacity growth leads to noise fitting Benign overfitting via smooth interpolators
Generalization Curve Monotonic U-curve Double Descent curve with second descent phase

Appendix: Step-by-Step Rigorous Proof of Hoeffding’s Inequality

Hoeffding’s Inequality bounds the probability that the empirical mean of independent, bounded random variables deviates from its expected value.

Step 1: The Chernoff Bound Technique (Markov’s Inequality)

Let $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N (X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_n])$, where $X_n \in [a_n, b_n]$ are independent random variables. For any strictly positive real parameter $s > 0$:

$$ P\left( \frac{1}{N} S_N \ge \varepsilon \right) = P(S_N \ge N\varepsilon) = P\left( e^{s S_N} \ge e^{s N \varepsilon} \right) $$

Applying Markov’s inequality ($P(Y \ge c) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[Y]}{c}$ for non-negative $Y$):

$$ P(S_N \ge N\varepsilon) \le e^{-s N \varepsilon} \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{s S_N} \right] $$

Since all variables $X_n$ are mutually independent, the expectation of their exponentiated sum factorizes into the product of their individual moment-generating functions:

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{s S_N} \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \exp\left( \sum_{n=1}^N s(X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_n]) \right) \right] = \prod_{n=1}^N \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{s(X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_n])} \right] $$

Step 2: Hoeffding’s Lemma (Bounding the MGF of a Zero-Mean Variable)

Lemma (Hoeffding’s Lemma). If $Z$ is a real-valued random variable with $\mathbb{E}[Z] = 0$ and $Z \in [a, b]$, then for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$:

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{sZ} \right] \le \exp\left( \frac{s^2(b - a)^2}{8} \right) $$

Proof. Because $f(z) = e^{sz}$ is convex, its chord between $a$ and $b$ lies above the curve for all $z \in [a, b]$:

$$ e^{sz} \le \frac{b - z}{b - a} e^{sa} + \frac{z - a}{b - a} e^{sb} $$

Taking expectations on both sides, utilizing $\mathbb{E}[Z] = 0$:

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[ e^{sZ} \right] \le \frac{b}{b - a} e^{sa} - \frac{a}{b - a} e^{sb} = (1 - \theta + \theta e^{s(b-a)}) e^{-\theta s(b-a)} \triangleq e^{\phi(u)} $$

where $\theta = \frac{-a}{b - a}$, $u = s(b - a)$, and $\phi(u) = -\theta u + \ln(1 - \theta + \theta e^u)$. Evaluating derivatives of $\phi(u)$:

$$ \begin{aligned} \phi(0) &= 0 \\ \phi'(u) &= -\theta + \frac{\theta e^u}{1 - \theta + \theta e^u} \implies \phi'(0) = 0 \\ \phi''(u) &= \frac{\theta e^u (1 - \theta)}{(1 - \theta + \theta e^u)^2} = p(1 - p) \le \frac{1}{4} \quad \left(\text{where } p = \frac{\theta e^u}{1 - \theta + \theta e^u}\right) \end{aligned} $$

By Taylor’s theorem with Lagrange remainder around $u = 0$:

$$ \phi(u) = \phi(0) + \phi'(0)u + \frac{1}{2} \phi''(\xi) u^2 \le 0 + 0 + \frac{1}{8} u^2 = \frac{s^2 (b - a)^2}{8} $$

Exponentiating both sides yields $\mathbb{E}[e^{sZ}] \le \exp\left( \frac{s^2(b - a)^2}{8} \right)$. $\blacksquare$

Step 3: Combining and Optimizing the Free Parameter $s$

Substituting Hoeffding’s Lemma back into the Chernoff product:

$$ P(S_N \ge N\varepsilon) \le e^{-s N \varepsilon} \prod_{n=1}^N \exp\left( \frac{s^2 (b_n - a_n)^2}{8} \right) = \exp\left( -s N \varepsilon + \frac{s^2 \sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2}{8} \right) $$

To minimize this upper bound with respect to $s > 0$, we differentiate the quadratic exponent $g(s) = -s N \varepsilon + \frac{s^2 \sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2}{8}$ and set it to zero:

$$ g'(s) = -N\varepsilon + \frac{s \sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2}{4} = 0 \implies s^* = \frac{4 N \varepsilon}{\sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2} $$

Plugging this optimal $s^*$ back into the exponent:

$$ g(s^*) = -\frac{4 N^2 \varepsilon^2}{\sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2} + \frac{16 N^2 \varepsilon^2 \sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2}{8 \left( \sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2 \right)^2} = -\frac{2 N^2 \varepsilon^2}{\sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2} $$

Step 4: Specialization to Normalized Losses in $[0, 1]$

In standard statistical learning, losses are normalized such that $\ell \in [0, 1]$. Thus, $b_n - a_n = 1 - 0 = 1$, giving $\sum_{n=1}^N (b_n - a_n)^2 = N$. The one-sided tail bound reduces to:

$$ P\left( \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N X_n - \mathbb{E}[X] \ge \varepsilon \right) \le \exp(-2N\varepsilon^2) $$

By symmetry, the lower tail satisfies $P\left( \mathbb{E}[X] - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N X_n \ge \varepsilon \right) \le \exp(-2N\varepsilon^2)$. Applying the union bound across both tails produces the full two-sided Hoeffding’s Inequality:

$$ P\left( \left| \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N X_n - \mathbb{E}[X] \right| \ge \varepsilon \right) \le 2\exp(-2N\varepsilon^2) $$

$\blacksquare$

item.title: From Linear Regression to Deep Neural Networks
item.description:
Linear Models & Loss Formulations

From Simple to Multiple Linear Regression

A simple linear model maps a single scalar feature $x_1$ via an affine transformation:

$$ y = b + w x_1 $$

When scaling from a single input to $D$ distinct input features $\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2, \dots, x_D]^T$, the model generalizes to Multiple Linear Regression:

$$ y = b + \sum_{j=1}^D w_j x_j = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b $$
  • $w_j$ (Weight): Slope / partial derivative governing target response with respect to feature $x_j$.
  • $b$ (Bias): Intercept / baseline offset.
  • Geometric Interpretation: The model defines a flat, non-curving hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^{D+1}$. It cannot capture interactions or non-linear behaviors without explicit transformations.

Loss Function Formulations: Regression and Classification

Given $M$ training samples $\{(\mathbf{x}^{(m)}, \hat{y}^{(m)})\}_{m=1}^M$, the loss function acts as a measurable metric evaluated over empirical errors.

1. Mean Squared Error (MSE / $L_2$ Loss) — Regression

$$ L_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left( \hat{y}_{\text{pred}}^{(m)} - \hat{y}^{(m)} \right)^2 $$

Smooth and differentiable everywhere, but sensitive to extreme outliers due to quadratic penalization.

2. Mean Absolute Error (MAE / $L_1$ Loss) — Regression

$$ L_{\text{MAE}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left| \hat{y}_{\text{pred}}^{(m)} - \hat{y}^{(m)} \right| $$

Robust to outliers, but features a discontinuous subgradient at zero residual ($e = 0$).

3. Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) — Binary Classification

For binary labels $\hat{y} \in \{0, 1\}$ paired with a sigmoid probability output $p \in (0, 1)$:

$$ L_{\text{BCE}} = - \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left[ \hat{y}^{(m)} \ln(p^{(m)}) + (1 - \hat{y}^{(m)}) \ln(1 - p^{(m)}) \right] $$

Acts as an algebraic switch: activates $-\ln(p)$ if $\hat{y}=1$, and $-\ln(1-p)$ if $\hat{y}=0$.

4. Categorical Cross-Entropy (CCE) — Multiclass Classification

For mutually exclusive classification across $C > 2$ classes, targets are one-hot encoded $\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{(m)} \in \{0, 1\}^C$. Raw logits are converted to normalized class probabilities using the Softmax function:

$$ p_c^{(m)} = \frac{e^{z_c^{(m)}}}{\sum_{k=1}^C e^{z_k^{(m)}}}, \quad \text{where } \sum_{c=1}^C p_c^{(m)} = 1 $$

The loss computes empirical cross-entropy over all classes:

$$ L_{\text{CCE}} = - \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \sum_{c=1}^C \hat{y}_c^{(m)} \ln\left( p_c^{(m)} \right) $$

Because only the true ground-truth class has $\hat{y}_c = 1$ while all others equal $0$, the inner summation isolates and penalizes solely the negative log probability of the correct class: $-\ln(p_{\text{correct}})$.

Optimization: Analytical Solution vs. Gradient Descent

Analytical Solution via Partial Derivatives (Normal Equation)

To find the minimum of an unconstrained convex loss surface, calculus dictates setting all directional slopes to zero simultaneously.

Scalar Setting: Two-Variable System

For simple linear regression $L(w, b) = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left( b + w x^{(m)} - \hat{y}^{(m)} \right)^2$, we compute the explicit partial derivatives:

$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial L}{\partial w} &= \frac{2}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left( b + w x^{(m)} - \hat{y}^{(m)} \right) x^{(m)} = 0 \\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} &= \frac{2}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left( b + w x^{(m)} - \hat{y}^{(m)} \right) = 0 \end{aligned} $$

Because this system is linear with respect to $w$ and $b$, it forms a standard solvable system of two linear equations.

Matrix Generalization: The Normal Equation

When generalized across $D$ features with unified vector $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{(D+1) \times 1}$, setting all simultaneous partial derivatives to zero yields the compact matrix formulation:

$$ \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w}^* = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} \implies \mathbf{w}^* = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} $$
  • Computational Bottleneck: Inverting the Gram matrix $(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})$ requires $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$ runtime complexity, becoming computationally intractable when the parameter dimension $d \gg 10^5$.
  • Non-linear Incompatibility: Once non-linear activation functions (e.g., Sigmoid, ReLU) are introduced, partial derivative equations turn into transcendental equations with no closed-form algebraic solutions.

Gradient Descent (GD) & Mini-Batch SGD

The Gradient Operator $\nabla$ as Vectorized Partial Derivatives

When parameters scale to an arbitrary collection $\boldsymbol{\theta} = [\theta_1, \theta_2, \dots, \theta_P]^T$, writing separate partial derivative equations becomes unmanageable. The gradient operator $\nabla$ (nabla) serves as unified vector notation packaging all dimensional partial derivatives into a single column vector:

$$ \nabla L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \triangleq \left[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_1}, \; \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_2}, \; \dots, \; \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_P} \right]^T $$

In standard Gradient Descent, parameters update iteratively in the direction of steepest descent:

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta \nabla L(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t) $$

where $\eta > 0$ denotes the learning rate.

Mini-Batch SGD & Iteration Step $k$

Computing gradients over the entire training set of $N$ instances simultaneously requires massive GPU memory. Modern training partitions the $N$ total samples into sequential mini-batches of size $B$.

Let the index $k \in \{1, 2, \dots\}$ denote the sequential iteration step consuming the $k$-th mini-batch:

$$ g = \nabla L^k(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k-1}), \quad \boldsymbol{\theta}^k \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^{k-1} - \eta g $$
  • $L^k$: The loss evaluated only on the data within the $k$-th mini-batch.
  • $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k-1}$: The model parameter vector obtained from the preceding step.
  • $\boldsymbol{\theta}^k$: The updated parameter vector after consuming batch $k$.
  • $1\text{ Epoch}$: Achieved when all batches covering the entire dataset $N$ have been processed once.

Stochastic mini-batch sampling bounds hardware memory footprints and introduces natural gradient noise, aiding escape from saddle points and shallow local traps.

Introducing Non-Linearity: Sigmoid and ReLU

Linear models cannot fit curved geometries. Non-linear activation functions bend hyperplanes into piecewise continuous surfaces.

The Logistic Sigmoid Function

$$ \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} $$

Produces an S-shaped smooth threshold. Arbitrary 1D non-linear curves can be approximated by summing multiple shifted and scaled sigmoids:

$$ y = b + \sum_{i} c_i \, \sigma(b_i + w_i x_1) $$

Figure 1 — Left: Effect of varying hyperparameters $w_i, b_i, c_i$ on a single sigmoid. Right: Piecewise non-linear curve assembly formed by summing multiple translated sigmoid units.

The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)

As shown by Prof. Hung-yi Lee, a continuous sigmoid can be approximated by two rectified piecewise linear ramps. In modern deep learning, the ReLU function is widely preferred:

$$ \text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z) $$
  • Computational Efficiency: Avoids costly exponential operations; evaluates via simple thresholding.
  • Mitigating Vanishing Gradients: For $z > 0$, the derivative is strictly constant ($\frac{d}{dz}\text{ReLU}(z) = 1$), avoiding the vanishing gradient saturation inherent to sigmoid tails ($\sigma'(z) \to 0$ for $|z| \gg 0$).

Multi-Feature Input & The Artificial Neuron

By bridging Multiple Linear Regression ($\sum_j w_j x_j$) with non-linear activation functions ($\sigma$), we establish the foundational Artificial Neuron.

Forward Computation of a Neuron

Each individual neuron $i$ accepts all $D$ input features, computes an affine inner product, and passes the result through an activation function:

$$ z_i = b_i + \sum_{j=1}^D w_{ij} x_j = \mathbf{w}_i^T \mathbf{x} + b_i, \quad a_i = \sigma(z_i) \text{ (or } \text{ReLU}(z_i)\text{)} $$

Figure 2 — Architecture of a fully connected single-hidden-layer neural network illustrating synaptic weight intersections ($w_{ij}$) and output aggregation weights ($c_i$).

Single-Hidden-Layer Network

Aggregating $K$ hidden units together with an output layer produces:

$$ y = b + \sum_{i=1}^K c_i \, \sigma\left( b_i + \sum_{j=1}^D w_{ij} x_j \right) $$
  • $w_{ij}$: Synaptic weight connecting input feature $j$ to hidden neuron $i$.
  • $c_i$: Weight scaling the contribution of neuron $i$ to the final output.
  • Universal Approximation Theorem: A single hidden layer with a sufficient finite number of non-linear neurons can approximate any continuous function on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^D$ to arbitrary precision.

Linear Algebra Formulation (Vectorized Representation)

For parallelized batch inference across $M$ samples:

  • Input data matrix: $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times D}$
  • Hidden weight matrix: $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times K}$
  • Hidden bias vector: $\mathbf{b}_h^T \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times K}$
  • Output weight vector: $\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 1}$
  • Output bias scalar: $b \in \mathbb{R}$

Vectorized execution pipeline:

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{Z} &= \mathbf{X} \mathbf{W} + \mathbf{1}_M \mathbf{b}_h^T \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K} \\ \mathbf{A} &= \sigma(\mathbf{Z}) \quad (\text{or } \max(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Z})) \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K} \\ \hat{\mathbf{y}} &= \mathbf{A} \mathbf{c} + b \mathbf{1}_M \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 1} \end{aligned} $$

Deep Neural Networks (Hierarchical Representation)

Rather than expanding width $K$ in a single layer, deep learning constructs functional compositions across $L$ stacked layers:

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}^{(1)} &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}^{(1)} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}) \\ \mathbf{h}^{(2)} &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}^{(2)} \mathbf{h}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}) \\ &\;\;\vdots \\ \hat{y} &= \mathbf{W}^{(L)} \mathbf{h}^{(L-1)} + b^{(L)} \end{aligned} $$

Architectural Advantages & Multi-Layer Diagram

Figure 3 — Architecture of a deep multi-layer neural network cascading through hierarchical intermediate representations.

  • Hierarchical Abstraction: Early layers isolate localized low-level primitives; deep layers recursively compose these into complex global manifolds.
  • Parameter Efficiency: Deep composition $f_L(\dots f_1(\mathbf{x}))$ achieves exponential expressivity with significantly fewer parameters than equivalent shallow wide architectures.
  • Backpropagation: Gradients across all layers are calculated via systematic recurrence of the multivariate chain rule:
$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}} $$

Model Diagnostics & Troubleshooting Guide

When empirical model performance is suboptimal, diagnosing the root cause requires systematic examination of the discrepancy between Training Loss and Testing/Validation Loss.

Figure 4 — Systematic decision-tree workflow for diagnosing model performance bottlenecks.

Phase 1: Diagnosing Large Training Loss

If training loss remains high, the model has failed to fit even the observed data:

  • Model Bias (Underfitting): The model family lacks the expressive capacity to fit the target surface. Remedy: Expand the hypothesis space by adding features, widening layers, or deepening the network.
  • Optimization Issue: The model possesses sufficient capacity, but gradient descent is trapped in a bad local flat region or exhibits numerical divergence. Remedy: Switch to adaptive optimizers (e.g., Adam), apply learning rate warmup/scheduling, or incorporate residual shortcut connections.

Phase 2: Diagnosing Large Testing Loss (Low Training Loss)

If training loss is low but testing loss diverges, the model lacks generalizability:

  • Overfitting: The model memorized sample-specific noise rather than generalizable underlying patterns. Remedy (The Fundamental Trade-off):
    1. Acquire more real data or apply Data Augmentation.
    2. Constrain model complexity: reduce neuron counts, apply weight decay ($L_2$ regularization), or apply Dropout.
    3. Use Cross-Validation on split training/validation partitions for principled model selection.
  • Data Mismatch: The training and testing sets originate from fundamentally different distributions (e.g., domain shift). Pure structural adjustments cannot resolve mismatch; domain adaptation or aligned data sampling is mandatory.

Appendix: Step-by-Step Derivation of the Normal Equation

This appendix provides an intuitive mathematical bridge explaining how setting all directional gradients to zero directly transforms into the closed-form matrix solution $\mathbf{w}^* = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$.

Part 1. Unpacking the Matrix Notation

To absorb the bias term $b$ directly into $\mathbf{w}$, we augment the feature space by appending a dummy feature $x_0 = 1$ to each sample. For $M$ training samples and $D$ features:

$$ \mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_{11} & \cdots & x_{1D} \\ 1 & x_{21} & \cdots & x_{2D} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{M1} & \cdots & x_{MD} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times (D+1)}, \quad \mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} b \\ w_1 \\ \vdots \\ w_D \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{(D+1) \times 1}, \quad \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{y}^{(1)} \\ \hat{y}^{(2)} \\ \vdots \\ \hat{y}^{(M)} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 1} $$

The residual error vector $\mathbf{e}$ representing sample-wise deviations is:

$$ \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\mathbf{w} - \hat{y}^{(1)}) \\ \vdots \\ (\mathbf{x}^{(M)}\mathbf{w} - \hat{y}^{(M)}) \end{bmatrix} $$

Part 2. Expanding the Total Loss Function

The sum of squared errors is equivalent to the inner product of the residual vector with itself:

$$ \begin{aligned} L(\mathbf{w}) &= \mathbf{e}^T \mathbf{e} \\ &= (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y})^T (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}) \\ &= \left( (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w})^T - \mathbf{y}^T \right) (\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}) \\ &= \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w} - \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y} \end{aligned} $$

Because the scalar term $\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$ equals its transpose $\mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w}$, the two middle cross-terms merge:

$$ L(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{w}^T (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}) \mathbf{w} - 2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y})^T \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y} $$

Part 3. Calculating the Gradient

To minimize $L(\mathbf{w})$, we differentiate with respect to the parameter vector $\mathbf{w}$ term by term:

  1. Constant Term: $\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{w}} (\mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{0}$
  2. Linear Term: $\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{w}} \left( 2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y})^T \mathbf{w} \right) = 2 \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$
  3. Quadratic Term: $\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{w}} \left( \mathbf{w}^T (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}) \mathbf{w} \right) = 2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}) \mathbf{w}$

Combining these yields the complete gradient vector $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L$:

$$ \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L = 2 \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w} - 2 \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} $$

Part 4. Setting Gradients to Zero and Solving

At the optimal parameter configuration $\mathbf{w}^*$, setting the gradient to zero:

$$ 2 \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w}^* - 2 \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0} \implies (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}) \mathbf{w}^* = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} $$

Pre-multiplying both sides by the inverse matrix $(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}$:

$$ \mathbf{w}^* = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} $$

item.title: Evaluation Metrics Comprehensive Guide
item.description:
1. Core Concepts and Classification Framework

Prediction vs Ground Truth Variable Types

Format Description
Hard label / Discrete decision Final classification output, e.g., 0/1, “cat”/“dog”
Soft score / Continuous value Probability, confidence, logit, distance, ranking score
Format Description
Binary classification (discrete) 0/1, most common
Multiclass classification (discrete) 3+ mutually exclusive classes
Continuous real values e.g., temperature, price, rating exact values
Ordinal / Graded Between binary and continuous, e.g., relevance scoring 0-5
Structured labels Segmentation mask, bounding box, ranked list
Probability distribution / Soft labels GT itself is a probability distribution, e.g., knowledge distillation

Important: Almost all “hard label metrics” (Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1…) can accept continuous scores as input in code — but that’s because the code performs an implicit thresholding behind the scenes (usually threshold=0.5). This does not mean these metrics “support” continuous predictions. If your prediction is continuous, you must first choose a threshold to convert it to a hard label before computing these metrics. Threshold selection directly affects results, which is why threshold-free metrics like AUROC / AUPRC are more favored in papers.

Basic symbols: TP=True Positive, FP=False Positive, TN=True Negative, FN=False Negative, N=total samples, P=Precision, R=Recall, $p_i$=predicted probability of sample $i$, $y_i$=true label of sample $i$, $\hat{y}_i$=regression prediction

2. Overview Matrix

GT \ Pred Pred = Hard label / Discrete Pred = Continuous score / Probability
GT=Binary Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, MCC, Kappa, Specificity, G-mean, IoU AUROC, AUPRC/AP, Log Loss, Brier Score, KS statistic, Gini coefficient
GT=Multiclass Multiclass Accuracy, Macro/Micro/Weighted-F1, Confusion Matrix Multiclass AUROC(OvR/OvO), Top-k Accuracy, Cross-Entropy(NLL)
GT=Continuous (rare, requires discretizing GT first) MSE, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, R², Pearson r, Spearman ρ, Kendall τ, CCC, ICC
GT=Ordinal Weighted Kappa NDCG, Kendall τ, Spearman ρ
GT=Structured(mask/box/sequence) IoU, Dice, Pixel Accuracy mAP(detection), Panoptic Quality, MAP/MRR/NDCG(retrieval)
GT=Probability distribution — KL divergence, JS divergence, Cross-entropy, Wasserstein distance, CRPS, Perplexity

3. Binary Classification · Hard Label Metrics

Requirement: GT = binary discrete(0/1); Pred = discrete hard label(0/1)

3.1 Confusion Matrix 

 GT=1 GT=0
Pred=1 TP FP
Pred=0 FN TN
Metric Formula Description
Accuracy $\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$ Distorts under class imbalance, not recommended as sole metric
Precision (PPV) $\frac{TP}{TP+FP}$ Proportion of predicted positives that are truly positive
Recall / Sensitivity / TPR $\frac{TP}{TP+FN}$ Proportion of true positives correctly identified
Specificity / TNR $\frac{TN}{TN+FP}$ Proportion of true negatives correctly identified
F1-score $\frac{2PR}{P+R} = \frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN}$ Harmonic mean of Precision and Recall
F-$\beta$ score $\frac{(1+\beta^2)PR}{\beta^2P+R}$ $\beta>1$ weights Recall more, $\beta<1$ weights Precision more
F$_{0.5}$-score $\beta=0.5$ More emphasis on Precision
F$_2$-score $\beta=2$ More emphasis on Recall
Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) $\frac{TP\cdot TN-FP\cdot FN}{\sqrt{(TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)}}$ More robust than F1 under imbalance, range [-1,1]
Cohen’s Kappa $\frac{p_o-p_e}{1-p_e}$ Agreement corrected for chance, -1~1
Balanced Accuracy $\frac{\text{Sensitivity}+\text{Specificity}}{2}$ Improved Accuracy for imbalanced data
G-mean $\sqrt{\text{Sensitivity} \times \text{Specificity}}$ Also for imbalanced data
Jaccard index / IoU $\frac{\|A \cap B\|}{\|A \cup B\|} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP+FN}$ Also used in image segmentation
Youden’s J (Informedness) $\text{Sensitivity}+\text{Specificity}-1$ Often used to find optimal ROC threshold, -1~1
Markedness $\text{PPV}+\text{NPV}-1$ Dual to Informedness (prediction perspective)
NPV $\frac{TN}{TN+FN}$ Proportion of predicted negatives that are truly negative
FPR $\frac{FP}{FP+TN} = 1-\text{Specificity}$ False positive rate
FNR $\frac{FN}{FN+TP} = 1-\text{Recall}$ False negative rate
Fall-out $\frac{FP}{FP+TN}$ Same as FPR
Miss rate $\frac{FN}{FN+TP}$ Same as FNR
FDR $\frac{FP}{TP+FP} = 1-\text{Precision}$ False discovery rate
Hamming Loss $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{M}\mathbb{I}(y_i \neq \hat{y}_i)$ 0~1, smaller is better, M=number of labels

F1 and harmonic mean: Harmonic mean is more sensitive to extreme values, so F1 requires both Precision and Recall to be high for a high score. If they differ greatly, F1 will be significantly lower than the arithmetic mean.

4. Binary Classification · Continuous Score (Threshold-Free) Metrics

Requirement: GT = binary discrete(0/1); Pred = continuous score / probability

4.1 ROC and AUC Series

Metric Definition Description
AUROC / ROC-AUC Area under ROC curve (TPR vs FPR) Insensitive to class imbalance, but may be overly optimistic in extreme imbalance
AUPRC / PR-AUC / Average Precision (AP) Area under PR curve (Precision vs Recall) More reflective of true performance than AUROC in extreme imbalance (e.g., rare disease detection)
Gini coefficient $2 \times \text{AUROC} - 1$ Commonly used in credit scoring, equivalent information to AUROC
Partial AUC AUC within a specified FPR or TPR range Used when only a specific operating range matters
tAUC (truncated AUC) Truncated AUC Focus on high TPR or high FPR regions
Lift Proportion of positives captured in top k% vs random Common in marketing / risk control

AUPRC computation pitfall: Some people directly apply trapezoidal integration on PR curve points, but the PR curve is non-monotonic, yielding inflated/inaccurate values. The correct approach is the non-interpolated Average Precision definition (e.g., sklearn’s average_precision_score), not computing auc() on a drawn PR curve.

4.2 Probability Quality and Calibration Metrics

Metric Formula Description
Log Loss / Binary Cross-Entropy $-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[y_i \cdot \log(p_i) + (1-y_i) \cdot \log(1-p_i)]$ Penalizes both wrong direction and overconfidence
Brier Score $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(p_i - y_i)^2$ Mean squared error of probability predictions, lower is better
ECE (Expected Calibration Error) $\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{ B_m
MCE (Maximum Calibration Error) $\max_m \text{acc}(B_m)-\text{conf}(B_m)

4.3 Other Continuous Score Metrics

Metric Definition Description
KS statistic $\max_t \text{CDF}{\text{pos}}(t) - \text{CDF}{\text{neg}}(t)

5. Multiclass Metrics

Requirement: GT = multiclass discrete (K classes, K≥3)

5.1 Per-Class and Aggregation

Metric Aggregation Description
Macro-Average Precision Arithmetic mean of per-class Precision Treats each class equally, small and large classes have equal weight
Macro-Average Recall Arithmetic mean of per-class Recall
Macro-F1 Arithmetic mean of per-class F1
Micro-Average Precision $\frac{\sum TP_c}{\sum TP_c + \sum FP_c}$ Treats each sample equally, dominated by large classes
Micro-Average Recall $\frac{\sum TP_c}{\sum TP_c + \sum FN_c}$
Micro-F1 F1 of Micro Precision and Micro Recall In multiclass, Micro-F1 = Accuracy
Weighted-Average Weighted by number of samples per class

5.2 Overall Metrics

Metric Description
Accuracy Proportion of correctly predicted samples
Cohen’s Kappa (multiclass) Agreement corrected for chance
Confusion Matrix K×K matrix, most informative but not a single scalar
Top-k Accuracy True class falls within top-k predicted classes, common in ImageNet
Log Loss / Cross-Entropy $-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{ic} \cdot \log(p_{ic})$

5.3 ROC Extensions in Multiclass

Metric Description
One-vs-Rest ROC-AUC (OVRA) Binary classification per class, then macro/micro average
One-vs-One ROC-AUC (OVOA) Binary classification between each pair of classes

Standard approach is One-vs-Rest (each class treated as “positive vs rest”) or One-vs-One, then macro or weighted average.

6. Multilabel Classification Metrics

Requirement: GT = vector of multiple binary labels (each sample can belong to multiple classes, labels are not mutually exclusive)

Metric Pred requirement Description
Hamming Loss Discrete multilabel vector Per-label error rate average
Subset Accuracy (Exact Match Ratio) Discrete multilabel vector All labels must match exactly, very strict
Macro/Micro-F1 (multilabel) Discrete multilabel vector Similar to multiclass but labels are not mutually exclusive
Label Ranking AP (LRAP) Continuous score vector Threshold-free version, evaluates whether relevant labels rank higher

7. Regression / Continuous Value Prediction Metrics

Requirement: GT = continuous real values; Pred = continuous real values

7.1 Error-Based Metrics

Metric Formula Description
MSE (Mean Squared Error) $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2$ Heavier penalty on large errors, unit is squared original unit
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) $\sqrt{\text{MSE}}$ Same unit as original variable, more intuitive
MAE (Mean Absolute Error) $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i-\hat{y}_i
MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error) $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left \frac{y_i-\hat{y}_i}{y_i}\right
sMAPE (symmetric MAPE) $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{2 y_i-\hat{y}_i
RMSLE (Root Mean Squared Log Error) $\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\log(y_i+1)-\log(\hat{y}_i+1))^2}$ Log error, suitable for long-tail distributions
Huber Loss ($\delta$) $\begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}(y-\hat{y})^2 & \text{if } e

7.2 R²-Based Metrics

Metric Formula Description
R² (Coefficient of Determination) $1 - \frac{SS_{\text{res}}}{SS_{\text{tot}}} = 1 - \frac{\sum(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2}$ Proportion of variance explained by the model, closer to 1 is better, can be negative
Adjusted R² $1 - (1-R^2)\frac{N-1}{N-p-1}$ R² corrected for number of predictors

7.3 Correlation Metrics

Metric Formula/Description Description
Pearson r $\frac{\text{Cov}(y,\hat{y})}{\sigma_y \cdot \sigma_{\hat{y}}}$ Measures linear correlation, does not measure numerical agreement (scale/offset differences still yield r=1)
Spearman ρ Pearson on ranks Measures monotonic relationship, robust to outliers
Kendall’s Tau τ Based on concordant/discordant pairs Also measures monotonic relationship, more robust for small samples
CCC (Concordance Correlation Coefficient) $\frac{2\rho\sigma_y\sigma_{\hat{y}}}{\sigma_y^2+\sigma_{\hat{y}}^2+(\mu_y-\mu_{\hat{y}})^2}$ Measures both correlation and agreement (corrects for offset and scale), common in medical/biostatistics

Pearson r vs CCC: Pearson r only measures linear correlation degree, not requiring predicted and true values to be numerically consistent (e.g., $\hat{y}=2y$ gives r=1). CCC considers both correlation and agreement (correction for offset and scale), thus stricter than r and more suitable for evaluating prediction accuracy.

7.4 Cross-Validation Related

Metric Description
CV Score (mean±std) Cross-validation R²/MSE etc.
LOO-CV MSE Leave-one-out
Paired t-test / Wilcoxon Model comparison

8. Survival Analysis / Risk Scoring

Requirement: GT = (event time t, event indicator δ); Pred = continuous risk score / survival function S(t)

Metric Description
C-index / Concordance Index Proportion of comparable pairs where predicted risk order matches actual
Time-dependent AUC AUC at specific time point t
Integrated AUC Integral average of AUC across multiple time points
Survival Brier Score Time-dependent Brier Score
Integrated Brier Score Time integral average

9. Probability Distribution / Density Estimation Metrics

Requirement: GT can be probability distribution or soft labels; Pred is also probability distribution or sampled samples

Metric Formula/Description Description
Log-Likelihood $\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p(x_i)$ Larger is better
Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) $-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p(x_i)$ Smaller is better
KL Divergence $D_{\text{KL}}(q\|p) = \int q(x)\log\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\,dx$ Asymmetric, measures information loss when approximating GT with Pred
JS Divergence $\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{\text{KL}}(q\|m)+\frac{1}{2}D_{\text{KL}}(p\|m)},\ m=\frac{p+q}{2}$ Symmetrized version of KL, has upper bound
Wasserstein Distance $L_p$ Wasserstein distance Commonly used to evaluate difference between generated and real distributions in GANs
CRPS (Continuous Ranked Probability Score) GT=single continuous value, Pred=full predictive distribution (CDF) Common in probabilistic weather forecasting / probabilistic regression

10. Ranking / Recommender Systems / Information Retrieval Metrics

Requirement: GT = relevance labels (binary or graded); Pred = ranked list (obtained by sorting continuous scores)

Metric GT requirement Description
MAP (Mean Average Precision) Binary relevance (0/1) Compute AP per query, then average across queries
MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) Binary relevance Only cares about position of first relevant result
NDCG@K Graded relevance (e.g., 0-5) The only classic ranking metric natively supporting graded GT
DCG@K Graded relevance Discounted Cumulative Gain
Precision@K Binary relevance Only look at top-k results
Recall@K Binary relevance

NDCG formula: $\text{DCG}@K = \sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{2^{rel_i}-1}{\log_2(i+1)}$, $\text{NDCG}@K = \frac{\text{DCG}@K}{\text{IDCG}@K}$, where IDCG is the DCG under ideal ranking.

11. Computer Vision: Object Detection Metrics

Requirement: GT = bounding box + class; Pred = box coordinates + class + continuous confidence score

Metric Description
IoU Intersection over Union
AP (Average Precision) AUC of PR curve at various IoU thresholds
AP@IoU=0.5 COCO standard
AP@IoU=0.75 COCO standard
mAP mean AP across classes
mAP@0.5:0.95 COCO standard, average of AP at IoU from 0.5 to 0.95 step 0.05

mAP@0.5:0.95 is the COCO detection benchmark standard, requiring AP computed at 10 different IoU thresholds (0.5, 0.55, …, 0.95) and then averaged. This is stricter than a single AP@0.5.

12. Computer Vision: Image Segmentation Metrics

Requirement: GT = pixel-level mask; Pred = pixel-level mask

Metric Formula/Description Description
IoU / Jaccard $\frac{TP}{TP+FP+FN}$ Most fundamental overlap measure for segmentation/detection
Dice coefficient / F1 $\frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN} = \frac{2\times\text{IoU}}{1+\text{IoU}}$ Mathematically equivalent to F1, most common in medical image segmentation
Pixel Accuracy Proportion of correctly classified pixels Distorts under class imbalance (large background, small foreground)
mIoU mean IoU across classes Most common metric for semantic segmentation
HAUSDOFF_95 95% Hausdorff distance Measures maximum boundary error, often reported alongside Dice

18. Common Pitfalls FAQ

Q1: My model outputs probabilities (continuous 0~1), but the paper requires F1-score. What to do?

You must first select a decision threshold (not necessarily 0.5), convert probabilities to 0/1 hard labels, then compute F1. Be sure to note the threshold selection method in the paper (e.g., selected on validation set to maximize F1, or using Youden’s J).

Q2: Ground truth is continuous scoring (e.g., 1-5 stars), can I directly compute AUROC?

No. Common approaches: ① Manually threshold the GT to binary (e.g., ≥4 stars = “positive”), then compute AUROC/AUPRC, but results depend on the threshold and must be stated; ② Use metrics suitable for ordinal/continuous GT: Spearman/Kendall’s tau, NDCG (ranking tasks), CCC/Pearson r (regression tasks).

Q3: Can Precision/Recall/F1 directly accept continuous predictions?

In engineering, yes (libraries typically auto-binomialize at 0.5 threshold), but this is implicit thresholding, not the metric being “designed to support” continuous inputs. If you don’t want to lose information due to a fixed threshold, prioritize threshold-free metrics like AUPRC/AUROC.

Q4: Is reporting a single metric in a paper sufficient?

Usually not enough. Recommended combination:

  • Imbalanced binary classification: AUPRC + F1 (at reasonable threshold) + AUROC, complementary
  • Balanced binary classification: Accuracy + AUROC usually sufficient
  • Regression: At least RMSE/MAE (interpretability) + R² or correlation coefficient (fit quality)
  • Model comparison: Supplement with statistical significance tests and confidence intervals
